subject: computing
title: KS3 Computing — Cybersecurity Protection & Safe Practices
subtitle: Firewalls, encryption, antivirus, 2FA, software updates, and safe digital practices.

data.targetWord: software or hardware that monitors network traffic and blocks connections that do not match permitted rules

examples.en-GB: The company's firewall blocked thousands of unauthorised connection attempts each day.

data.targetWord: the process of converting plaintext (readable data) into ciphertext (scrambled data) using an algorithm and a key so only authorised users can read it

examples.en-GB: Encryption ensures that even if an attacker intercepts your data, they cannot read it without the key.

data.targetWord: software that scans files and processes on a device, comparing them against a database of known malware signatures to detect and remove threats

examples.en-GB: The antivirus software detected and quarantined a suspicious file that had been downloaded by email.

data.targetWord: a software update that fixes a known security vulnerability or bug in a program

examples.en-GB: The company applied the security patch immediately to prevent attackers from exploiting the known vulnerability.

data.targetWord: a new version of software released by developers that may include security patches, bug fixes, and new features

examples.en-GB: Enabling automatic software updates ensures your device receives security patches as soon as they are released.

data.targetWord: a security process requiring users to provide two separate forms of identity verification before access is granted, such as a password and a one-time code

examples.en-GB: With 2FA enabled, an attacker who steals your password still cannot log in without the code sent to your phone.

data.targetWord: Virtual Private Network — software that creates an encrypted tunnel for all internet traffic from a device, masking the user's IP address and protecting data on public networks

examples.en-GB: Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi prevents attackers from intercepting your unencrypted data.

data.targetWord: Secure Sockets Layer — an encryption protocol that secures data transmitted between a browser and a web server; largely replaced by TLS but the term is still widely used

examples.en-GB: The bank's website uses SSL to ensure login credentials cannot be intercepted in transit.

data.targetWord: Transport Layer Security — the modern encryption protocol used by HTTPS to secure data in transit between browsers and servers, replacing the older SSL protocol

examples.en-GB: TLS ensures that data sent between your browser and a secure website is encrypted and cannot be read by third parties.

data.targetWord: HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure — the secure version of HTTP that uses SSL/TLS to encrypt all data exchanged between browser and web server

examples.en-GB: Always check for HTTPS and a padlock icon before entering passwords or payment details on a website.

data.targetWord: a secret string of characters used to authenticate a user's identity and grant access to a system, account, or device

examples.en-GB: A strong password uses a mixture of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols and is at least 12 characters long.

data.targetWord: software that generates, stores, and auto-fills unique, complex passwords for every account, secured in an encrypted vault requiring only one master password

examples.en-GB: Using a password manager means you can have a different strong password for every website without having to remember them all.

data.targetWord: a network security measure that configures a router or switch to only allow connections from devices whose MAC addresses have been pre-approved

examples.en-GB: The school network uses MAC address filtering to prevent unauthorised devices from connecting to the Wi-Fi.

data.targetWord: Service Set Identifier — the name of a Wi-Fi network that is broadcast publicly; hiding it means the network does not appear in lists of available networks

examples.en-GB: The home router's SSID was hidden so that casual users could not see the network, though this does not prevent determined attackers.

data.targetWord: a copy of data stored separately from the original so that it can be restored if the original is lost, corrupted, or encrypted by ransomware

examples.en-GB: Following the 3-2-1 rule, the organisation kept one backup stored offsite so ransomware could not reach it.

data.targetWord: the security principle that users should only be granted the minimum level of access rights needed to perform their role, limiting damage if an account is compromised

examples.en-GB: Under the principle of least privilege, a student account cannot install software or access other users' files.

data.targetWord: the process of verifying that a user is who they claim to be, typically through something they know, have, or are

examples.en-GB: Authentication using a fingerprint scanner is faster and more secure than a simple four-digit PIN.

data.targetWord: the process of determining what resources or actions an authenticated user is permitted to access or perform on a system

examples.en-GB: After authentication, authorisation controls determine whether the user can read, write, or delete files.

data.targetWord: the set of policies, practices, and technologies designed to protect a computer network and its data from unauthorised access, misuse, or attack

examples.en-GB: Network security measures include firewalls, encryption, MAC address filtering, and intrusion detection systems.

data.targetWord: a physical device, typically integrated into a router, that monitors and filters all network traffic entering and leaving an entire network

examples.en-GB: A hardware firewall sits between the internet and the internal network, protecting all devices on the network simultaneously.

data.targetWord: a program installed on an individual device that monitors and filters that specific device's incoming and outgoing network traffic

examples.en-GB: Windows Defender includes a software firewall that protects the individual laptop even when used away from the office.

data.targetWord: data that has been encrypted and appears as meaningless characters; it cannot be read without the correct decryption key

examples.en-GB: An attacker who intercepts the message will only see ciphertext, which is unreadable without the key.

data.targetWord: data in its original, readable form before encryption has been applied

examples.en-GB: The message was plaintext before being encrypted; only the intended recipient could convert the ciphertext back to plaintext.

data.targetWord: the process of converting ciphertext back into readable plaintext using the correct key

examples.en-GB: Only the recipient with the private key can perform decryption and read the original message.

data.targetWord: a piece of data used by an encryption algorithm to convert plaintext into ciphertext or ciphertext back into plaintext

examples.en-GB: Without the correct encryption key, the stolen data file is completely unreadable.

data.targetWord: a database maintained by antivirus software containing unique code patterns of known malware, used to identify infected files

examples.en-GB: The antivirus signature database must be updated regularly to recognise the latest known malware threats.

data.targetWord: the isolation of a suspected malicious file by antivirus software so it cannot cause harm while it is being investigated or awaiting removal

examples.en-GB: The antivirus placed the infected download in quarantine to prevent it from spreading to other files.

data.targetWord: a previously unknown software vulnerability that is being exploited by attackers before the developer has had a chance to release a fix

examples.en-GB: Antivirus software cannot protect against a zero-day attack because there is no signature in its database yet.

data.targetWord: a physical or behavioural characteristic unique to an individual — such as a fingerprint, face, or iris pattern — used as an authentication factor

examples.en-GB: Biometric authentication using a fingerprint scan is an example of 'something you are' as a second factor.

data.targetWord: the mechanisms and policies that restrict which users can access which resources or perform which actions on a system

examples.en-GB: Access control on the school network prevents students from accessing staff files or installing software.

data.sentence: A firewall monitors and ____ incoming and outgoing network traffic based on a set of rules.
A hardware firewall protects the entire ____ by sitting between the internet and internal devices.
A software firewall is installed on an individual ____ and only protects that specific machine.
Antivirus software works by comparing files against a ____ of known malware signatures.
Encryption converts ____ (readable data) into ciphertext that cannot be read without the key.
HTTPS uses ____ to encrypt data passing between a browser and a web server.
Two-factor authentication requires users to provide ____ separate forms of identity verification.
Software ____ fix known security vulnerabilities and should be applied promptly to prevent exploitation.
The 3-2-1 backup rule states that one copy of data must be stored ____ or off-network to protect against ransomware.
A VPN creates an encrypted ____ for all internet traffic, hiding the user's IP address.
The principle of least ____ means users only receive the minimum access rights needed for their role.
If antivirus detects a suspicious file it places it in ____ to prevent it spreading to other files.
A ____ attack exploits a vulnerability before the developer has released a fix, so antivirus has no signature for it.
A ____ manager generates and stores unique complex passwords for each account in an encrypted vault.
Encryption in ____ protects data while it is being sent across a network, for example via HTTPS.
Encryption at ____ protects data stored on a device, such as an encrypted hard drive on a stolen laptop.
MAC address ____ only allows devices with pre-approved hardware addresses to connect to a network.
Using a ____ means a stolen password alone is not enough for an attacker to access your account.
Credential stuffing uses stolen usernames and passwords to attempt logins on ____ websites.
A strong password should be at least ____ characters long and mix letters, numbers, and symbols.
Something you ____ is a biometric authentication factor — for example, a fingerprint or face scan.
The 3-2-1 backup rule requires three copies of data across two different storage ____ with one copy offsite.

data.title: How 2FA login works
data.instruction: Arrange these steps in the correct order to show how two-factor authentication works.
items: User enters their username and password
System verifies the password is correct
System sends a one-time code to the user's phone or authenticator app
System verifies the code and grants access

data.title: How HTTPS encryption protects data in transit
data.instruction: Arrange these steps in the correct order to show how HTTPS protects data sent over a network.
items: Browser requests a secure connection to the web server
Server sends its SSL/TLS certificate to the browser
Browser verifies the certificate is valid and trusted
Browser and server agree on an encryption key
All data sent between browser and server is encrypted using that key
An interceptor sees only meaningless ciphertext

data.instruction: Sort each scenario into whether it describes encryption in transit or encryption at rest.

pairs.text: HTTPS encrypting data between a browser and a web server
A VPN encrypting all traffic sent over public Wi-Fi
Encrypting an email as it travels between mail servers

Reusing the same password on multiple websites

Using your date of birth as a PIN

Using a password manager to generate and store passwords
Making a password at least 12 characters long
